passage: At their school in Nagpur, a brown stray dog had started sleeping under the stairs, and the principal allowed it to stay if the eco-club looked after it. Payal, eleven, signed up for water duty before anyone else. Every morning she filled the steel bowl, checked it hadn't been knocked over at lunch, and wrote "done" on the chart by the staffroom. When Eshaan forgot his turn on Friday, she didn't complain to Ma'am. She just did it and reminded him, "Monday's yours, okay? She drinks a lot when it's hot." Eshaan nodded and wrote it on his hand.

qa.q: Where did the stray dog sleep?
qa.a: Under the stairs.

qa.q: Why didn't Payal complain to Ma'am when Eshaan forgot?
qa.a: She seemed to care more that the dog had water than about blaming anyone, and trusted a reminder would work.

qa.q: How could the eco-club make the duty easier to remember?
qa.a: Put up a simple rota everyone passes, or pair children so one can remind the other.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after Payal quietly covers his turn?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed but grateful, and more likely to remember Monday because she didn't shame him.

grounding: It shows a girl taking active responsibility for a school animal and a group duty.

passage: I'm Bhupen, Leela's older brother. Since a new boy from Assam joined her Class 5, Leela has taken him on like a job. He doesn't speak much Hindi yet. I've seen her at the school gate drawing pictures in the dust to show which bus is his. At home she made him a list of useful words, "water," "toilet," "late," each with a drawing. When her friends went to play, she stayed back and ate lunch with him. I don't know if she likes him or if the teacher asked her. But she says "my buddy" in a very proud way.

qa.q: Which words did Leela put on the list?
qa.a: "Water," "toilet" and "late," each with a drawing.

qa.q: What does Leela saying "my buddy" in a proud way suggest?
qa.a: She seems to take real pride in the role and to care about helping him feel at home.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Leela so she doesn't carry it all?
qa.a: Add another buddy or two, so the new boy has more friends and Leela still gets time with her own.

qa.q: How might the new boy experience Leela's help?
qa.a: It probably makes a strange new school feel less lonely and confusing.

grounding: It shows, from a brother's view, a girl taking responsibility for helping a new classmate settle in.

passage:
Monday: Karthik, twelve, found a pigeon on the terrace that couldn't fly, one wing drooping. His sister Jyoti said, "Leave it, it'll die." He put it in a shoebox with a cloth and a bowl of water and asked Amma to call the animal helpline.
Wednesday: The volunteer had said to keep it quiet and warm until they could collect it. Karthik checked the box before and after school, speaking softly and not touching it.
Saturday: The volunteers came. Karthik carried the box down himself, then asked, "Do you need helpers on Sundays?" The next week, Jyoti went to the shelter with him.

qa.q: What did Karthik put the pigeon in?
qa.a: A shoebox with a cloth and a bowl of water.

qa.q: Why did Karthik ask about helping on Sundays?
qa.a: Caring for the pigeon made him want to keep helping animals, not just this one.

qa.q: Which of Karthik's choices kept the pigeon safest?
qa.a: Asking Amma to call the helpline and following the volunteer's advice to keep it quiet, instead of handling it himself.

qa.q: How did Jyoti's view change?
qa.a: She first said to leave it, but after seeing her brother's care she went to the shelter too. 🙂

grounding: It shows a boy taking active responsibility for an injured animal over a week and wanting to keep serving.

passage: Sit, beta, I'll tell you about your mother when she was ten. Shreya was the class monitor that year, and a thin brown dog used to sleep under the school stairs. Most children threw it a biscuit and forgot. Not Shreya. She made a chart on the back of her notebook: who brings the water bowl, who brings rotis, which day. Her friend Jaya took Tuesdays and Fridays. When the peon grumbled about the mess, Shreya and Jaya swept that corner themselves every evening before going home. By winter the dog followed the whole class to the gate. I still have that chart somewhere, folded in my cupboard.

qa.q: Where did the brown dog sleep?
qa.a: It slept under the school stairs.

qa.q: What does Shreya sweeping the corner herself suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt protective of the dog and saw it as her class's job, so rather than let the peon's complaint end the feeding, she fixed the mess herself.

qa.q: How could a teacher support children like Shreya who take on a job like this?
qa.a: A teacher could put the chart on the class wall and thank the helpers, so the duty is shared and does not all fall on one child.

qa.q: How might the peon have seen the dog feeding once the girls began sweeping?
qa.a: He probably found it less of a burden, since the mess was cleaned without him, and may have trusted the children more.

grounding: Illustrates a child taking steady responsibility for an animal and organising classmates into shared roles.

passage: The rain had been falling since lunch, and by four the school bus still had not come. Tanvir, eleven, had promised his teacher he would help Sarita this week, because her right arm was in a plaster and she could not carry her bag. Now the lane outside the gate was ankle-deep. He slung her bag across his chest over his own, took her umbrella in his free hand and held it over her cast instead of his head. 'Your shirt's soaked,' Sarita said. 'The plaster can't get wet. My shirt can,' he said. When the bus finally splashed up, he checked that she had a seat near the front before finding his own at the back, dripping and grinning.

qa.q: Why could Sarita not carry her own bag?
qa.a: Her right arm was in a plaster.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's reply about his shirt show about what he cared about most?
qa.a: It shows he cared more about keeping Sarita's plaster dry than about getting wet himself; he treated her comfort as his job that week. 🙂

qa.q: What small step could the school take so helpers like Tanvir are not stuck in the rain?
qa.a: The teacher could arrange a covered place to wait or a second helper, so the job stays safe and shared.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel about being helped this way?
qa.a: She might feel grateful and a little awkward, since she noticed he was getting soaked for her.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a peer-helper role he agreed to, even when heavy rain and a late bus make it harder.

passage: Four puppies had been born under the stairs of B-block, and their mother looked thin. Kunal, eleven, noticed first. He didn't wait for an adult to decide. He made a chart on the back of an old calendar: who brings water, who brings leftover rice, who checks the puppies after school. Six children signed up. Vijay, the watchman, said, "Don't let them into the lift." Kunal added that to the chart too. By the end of the week the puppies were rounder, and the chart had a seventh name.

qa.q: Where were the puppies born?
qa.a: Under the stairs of B-block.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when the chart got a seventh name?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and encouraged that more children were joining in.

qa.q: What would help Kunal keep this going safely?
qa.a: Ask an adult to help contact an animal welfare group, so the puppies can be checked and cared for properly.

qa.q: How might Vijay see the children's plan?
qa.a: He probably appreciates it but wants it kept orderly, which is why he added the lift rule.

grounding: Shows a child taking active responsibility for caring for animals and organising others in his colony.

passage:
"Ritu, give me your bag," said Chaitanya.
"I can carry it."
"With one arm in plaster? No. I'm your buddy this month anyway."
"Ma'am made you buddy?"
"I asked her." He swung the bag onto his shoulder. "I'll write your notes too, till your arm's better."
"Your handwriting's terrible."
"Then I'll write slowly." Chaitanya, ten, held the classroom door with his foot.
"Why are you doing all this?"
He shrugged. "You'd do it if I broke my arm."
Ritu smiled. "Fine. But I'm checking the spelling."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya offer to write for Ritu?
qa.a: Her notes.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have asked the teacher to be Ritu's buddy?
qa.a: He felt caring and responsible, wanting to help a classmate who was struggling.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Chaitanya in this role?
qa.a: Thank him and check in with both children so the help stays useful and not overwhelming.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel about Chaitanya's help?
qa.a: She's a bit proud at first, but grateful and amused by the end.

grounding: Shows a child volunteering for a helping role and caring for an injured classmate.

passage: I'm Avni, and last year I was house captain for the school camp. On the second night, a Class 3 boy, Ujjwal, sat outside his tent crying because he missed home. The other captains were busy with the campfire. I sat with him, told him about my first camp when I also cried, and walked him to the teacher on duty so he could phone his mother. Then I stayed until he fell asleep. Being captain wasn't about the badge. It was about noticing who needed help first.

qa.q: Why was Ujjwal crying outside his tent?
qa.a: He missed home.

qa.q: What does Avni staying until Ujjwal fell asleep suggest?
qa.a: Avni felt responsible for him and caring, wanting him to feel safe.

qa.q: What did Avni get right in helping Ujjwal?
qa.a: Avni comforted him, shared a similar story and took him to the teacher on duty to call home.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal remember Avni?
qa.a: As a kind older student who made a scary night feel safe.

grounding: Shows a child in a group role taking responsibility for a homesick younger student.

passage:
Class 5B note, Monday. By Eshaan Mathur, class teacher.
Since Tuvya came back with his leg in plaster, Chinmay has taken charge without being asked. He carries Tuvya's bag up the stairs every morning, saves him the seat near the door, and fetches his water bottle at break. Today, when the class lined up for the library, Chinmay asked if he could walk at the back "so Tuvya doesn't feel slow." He looked serious about it, almost like a job. I thanked him in front of the class and made him our official "helper of the week." I'll also check with Tuvya that he is comfortable with the help and not embarrassed by it.

qa.q: Where does Chinmay save Tuvya a seat?
qa.a: Near the door.

qa.q: What does Chinmay asking to walk at the back suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he feels caring and protective toward Tuvya, not wanting him to feel slow or left behind.

qa.q: What did Eshaan Mathur do next, and why check with Tuvya?
qa.a: He named Chinmay helper of the week and planned to check that Tuvya is comfortable, so the help doesn't embarrass him.

qa.q: How might Tuvya feel about all the help from Chinmay?
qa.a: Tuvya may feel grateful, but possibly a little self-conscious about needing it.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy taking responsibility for helping a classmate on crutches.

passage:
Wednesday. Shreya's diary.
There's a pigeon with a hurt wing on our building's terrace. Tejas from the fifth floor found it first. We put it in a shoebox with a cloth and a little water lid. I wanted to feed it bread, but Mummy said to ask someone who knows. She called the bird helpline number the society uses. A man is coming tomorrow morning to take it to the bird hospital. Tejas and I made a schedule to check on it: me before school, him after. I kept going up to look. It blinked at me! I feel responsible for it, like it's partly ours now.

qa.q: Where did they find the pigeon?
qa.a: On the building's terrace.

qa.q: How does Shreya feel about the pigeon?
qa.a: Shreya feels caring and responsible, as if the pigeon is partly theirs now.

qa.q: Which choice was wise, and why?
qa.a: Asking Mummy and calling the bird helpline instead of guessing what to feed, so it gets proper care.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about sharing the schedule?
qa.a: Tejas probably feels trusted and part of a team caring for the bird. 🙂

grounding: A child and a neighbour take responsibility for an injured pigeon with an adult's help.

passage: In the government school at Shirpur, the water pots had to be filled from the hand pump each morning. Nobody liked the job. Sumit, eleven, started doing it without being asked, then made a list so each pair of classmates got a day. He also noticed Arohi, the smallest girl in Class 2, couldn't lift the lid of the pot. He tied a string to it so she could pull it off herself. The headmistress saw the list on the wall and asked who made it. Sumit shrugged. "It was always empty." She smiled and put his name on the class board as water monitor.

qa.q: Where were the water pots filled from?
qa.a: From the hand pump.

qa.q: How did Sumit probably feel when the headmistress asked who made the list?
qa.a: He seemed modest and a little shy, shrugging instead of boasting.

qa.q: What was smart about Sumit's list?
qa.a: It shared the job fairly among classmates instead of leaving it to one person.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel about the string on the lid?
qa.a: Arohi likely feels grateful and more included, able to get water on her own.

grounding: A village boy takes on the class water duty, organises a rota and helps a younger child.

passage:
In Pablo's classroom in Seville, the class hamster, Bolita, needed someone to feed him every day. Nobody wanted the job because the cage smelled.

Pablo, ten, raised his hand. "I'll do it."

Every morning he came ten minutes early, filled the water bottle, added seeds and changed the sawdust on Fridays. When Jana, who was new and shy, watched him, he asked, "Do you want to help?" He showed her how to hold Bolita gently.

One Monday Bolita wasn't eating. Pablo told the teacher straight away, and she called the vet.

Bolita got better. Jana now feeds him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What did Pablo change on Fridays?
qa.a: He changed the sawdust on Fridays.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel when Bolita wasn't eating?
qa.a: Pablo felt worried and responsible, so he told the teacher straight away.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on Pablo's care for the class?
qa.a: The teacher could let Pablo keep leading the hamster rota and thank him for including Jana.

qa.q: How might Jana feel being asked to help?
qa.a: Jana likely felt welcomed and included, less shy in a new class.

grounding: A boy takes responsibility for the class hamster and includes a shy new classmate.

passage:
It was the first week of winter at the school in Dehradun, and the new girl, Lavanya, stood alone near the staff room, shivering in a thin sweater.

Preeti, eleven, was class monitor. She saw Lavanya's cold hands and walked over. "You're in 6B? Come, I'll show you."

She showed her the classroom, the water cooler and the library. At lunch, she found Lavanya a seat at her table and lent her the extra shawl from her bag.

At home time, Lavanya said, "Thank you." Preeti shrugged. "It's my job. And also, you looked cold."

qa.q: What did Preeti lend Lavanya?
qa.a: She lent her the extra shawl from her bag.

qa.q: Why did Preeti walk over to Lavanya?
qa.a: Preeti felt concerned when she saw Lavanya's cold hands and felt responsible for her as class monitor.

qa.q: How did Preeti take responsibility as class monitor?
qa.a: She noticed Lavanya, showed her around, found her a seat and shared her shawl.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Preeti after the first day?
qa.a: Lavanya would likely see her as kind and trustworthy, a first friend in the new school.

grounding: In winter, a class monitor takes responsibility for helping a cold, lonely new student settle in.

passage:
I'm Pankaj from the building opposite. This monsoon, I watched Sonali, who's eleven, take care of the stray dogs in our lane.

Every evening she brought rotis in a steel box. When the puppies were soaked, she got four other kids to collect cardboard and old sacks, and they made a shelter under the stairs.

She made a chart: who feeds, who cleans, which day. Even the watchman helped.

I don't know why she started. She never said. But the puppies waited for her at six every evening.

qa.q: What did Sonali bring every evening?
qa.a: She brought rotis in a steel box.

qa.q: What might Sonali have been feeling as she cared for the puppies?
qa.a: Pankaj wasn't sure, but she seemed caring and determined, perhaps worried about the puppies getting soaked.

qa.q: How could the adults in the building support Sonali's group?
qa.a: They could provide a dry spot and old blankets, and help her contact an animal welfare group if a dog gets sick.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Sonali's effort?
qa.a: Pankaj is impressed and curious, noticing how she organised others without explaining why.

grounding: A neighbour observes a girl organising other children to care for stray dogs during the monsoon.

passage:
First cold night of December: Parveen heard whimpering under the colony water tank and found three puppies shivering. She and Trisha lined a carton with an old sweater.
Three days later: Parveen pinned a chart on the notice board: "Puppy duty: morning milk, Parveen; evening water, Trisha; check blanket, Sahil." Sahil forgot on Tuesday, so Parveen did his turn and reminded him kindly.
The next Sunday: The residents' secretary saw the chart and asked Parveen to speak at the meeting. Her voice shook, but she asked for a proper shelter box and a vet visit. Trisha held up the chart. Two uncles offered to build the box.

qa.q: What did Parveen and Trisha line the carton with?
qa.a: They lined it with an old sweater.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when her voice shook at the meeting?
qa.a: She was nervous speaking to adults but determined to get proper care for the puppies.

qa.q: What helped the puppy care keep going?
qa.a: Parveen shared duties on a clear chart, covered a missed turn kindly, and asked adults for bigger help like a vet visit.

qa.q: How does Trisha support Parveen at the meeting?
qa.a: Trisha holds up the chart, backing Parveen's request so Parveen isn't standing alone.

grounding: Shows a child taking responsibility for stray puppies in winter and organising others to help.
